title: Explicit expression and fast algorithms for the inverse of some matrices arising from implicit time integration

predicted_errors.error_location: Eq. (2.9) (definition of the generalized binomial coefficient at i = 0)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: (2.9) defines binom(c_n,c_0) = (-1)^n ∏_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_n-c_k) / ∏_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_{n-k}-c_0). Since ∏_{k=0}^{n-1}(c_{n-k}-c_0)=∏_{k=1}^{n}(c_k-c_0), this gives, for c_i=i, (-1)^n·n!/n! = (-1)^n, not 1 = binom(n,0), contradicting the immediately following assertion 'Setting c_n=n and c_i=i, it is clear that binom(c_n,c_i) is the binomial coefficient n!/(i!(n-i)!)'. It is also off by a factor (-1)^n from the value obtained by extending (2.8) to i=0, which is the value needed for Theorem 2.2 to hold (checked explicitly for n=1, where (2.9) gives -1 instead of 1).

The lemma states the value equals ∏_{k=0,k≠j}^{n}(c_j-c_k) for i≠j, but the proof (setting x=c_j in (2.7)) correctly obtains ∏_{k=0,k≠i,j}^{n}(c_j-c_k), i.e. the factor (c_j-c_i) must also be omitted. The lemma statement is therefore wrong by a factor (c_j-c_i) and inconsistent with its own proof and with Theorem 2.2 (where W_{ij} contains the extra prefactor 1/(c_j-c_i)).

(2.18) writes H^T = F [[0, c_0^T],[c_0, C_n]], using the node matrix C_n = diag(c_1,...,c_n). Since H has 1,2,...,n on its subdiagonal, H^T = F diag(0,1,2,...,n) = F [[0,0],[0,D_n]]. Indeed, the very next computation (2.19) uses D_n, not C_n, so (2.18) is internally inconsistent and mathematically wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Definition of σ preceding Eq. (2.2) (and the analogous statement in Lemma 2.1)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says 'σ_{n+1-k} denotes the kth elementary symmetric function of c_0,…,c_n, i.e., σ_{n+1-k}(c_0,…,c_n) is the sum of all distinct products of k of the arguments'. With φ(x)=∏_{k=0}^n(x-c_k)=Σ(-1)^{n+1-k}σ_{n+1-k}x^k, one needs σ_m = e_m (the sum of products of m arguments), so σ_{n+1-k} is the (n+1−k)th elementary symmetric function, not the kth. The same mis-indexing appears in the statement of Lemma 2.1 ('Let σ_{n-k} be the kth elementary symmetric function').

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction (claim about BIM matrix) vs. end of Section 2.2
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The introduction states 'the inverse of IRK matrix and BIM matrix is exactly W_n^T if c_i are the zeros of the Legendre polynomials and c_i = i, respectively'. But Section 2.2 gives the inverse of the BIM matrix as N = D_n (V_n D_n V_n^{-1} D_n^{-1}) D_n^{-1} + D_n^{-1}, i.e. a similarity transform of W_n^T (= V_n D_n V_n^{-1} C_n^{-1} with C_n = D_n when c_i=i) plus the extra term D_n^{-1}. Hence N ≠ W_n^T, and the introductory claim overstates the result.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Introduction ('our algorithms are both highly efficient and accurate')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper itself states that Algorithm 3.1 'is numerically unstable and inaccurate due to the rapid propagation of roundoff errors' and may overflow, and Section 4.2 tests only Algorithms 3.2 and 3.3 ('Now we will test the performance of Algorithms 3.2 and 3.3'). The blanket claim that all three proposed algorithms are 'highly efficient and accurate' is therefore unsupported and self-contradictory.

Example 3 defines c_i = 1/2 + 1/2 cos((2i+1)π/(2n+1)) for i = 0,...,n and labels them 'Chebyshev nodes in (0,1)'. For i = n the argument is exactly π, giving c_n = 0, which is not in the open interval (0,1). Chebyshev–Gauss nodes for n+1 points require the denominator 2n+2, not 2n+1.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2.2 (node-defining polynomials) and Example 2 in Section 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Radau IIA nodes are written as the zeros of 'd^n/dx^{n-1}(x^{n-1}(x-1)^n)', a malformed/incorrect differential operator; the correct Rodrigues-type expression is d^{n-1}/dx^{n-1}(x^{n-1}(x-1)^n). The same wrong expression is repeated in Example 2.

The stated component costs are: G costs (n+1)^2, g̃ costs 2n^2, W̃ costs n^2+n, and computing W from W̃ costs 3n^2+7n. These sum to 7n^2+10n+1, not the claimed '7n^2+9n flops'. (By contrast, the corresponding sum for Algorithm 3.2 reproduces its stated 7n^2+15n, showing the accounting for Algorithm 3.3 is inconsistent.)

The text claims 'From Remark 1, we see that the heavy cancellation does not occur in the sum since there exist no nearly equal numbers are subtracted from each other.' Remark 1 gives W_ii = Σ_{p=1}^{i}1/p − Σ_{p=1}^{n-i}1/p, i.e. the difference of two harmonic partial sums which are nearly equal (and exactly equal when i = n/2, giving W_ii = 0). Severe cancellation therefore does occur for i near n/2, contradicting the stated justification for the reported high componentwise relative accuracy.

'it requires less memory since A^{-1} ⊗ M is in general sparser than A ⊗ K' is not justified: A^{-1} is generally as dense as A, and the mass matrix M has essentially the same sparsity pattern as the stiffness matrix K in finite-element discretizations, so the stated memory argument attributed to [24] does not follow.
